lesson.subtitle: Lesson 18 -- Midpoint Review
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Denise Gadelha Rocha | Lesson 18 -- Midpoint Review
lesson.grammar_point: integrated review of the full grammar arc

listenings.text: Most people arrive at a midpoint review with a feeling and a list. The feeling is that it is going well, and the list is how much they have done. Neither of those is evidence, and I have stopped asking for them. What I count is narrower. Name a situation you could not handle at the start, tell me when you handled it, and tell me who was in the room. One of those is worth more to me than a whole term of activity. The second thing I would say is about plateaus. Almost everybody is on one at the halfway mark, and it is not a failure. It is what learning looks like once the easy gains are gone. The mistake people make there is to add something new, when what is half-built is the thing that needs to be made solid. The second half of any plan is not for learning more. It is for making what already exists hold under pressure.

For about four months in the middle of it, I improved in nothing. I was working as hard as I ever had, and all of that work was going into the parts that were already automatic. That is what a plateau actually is. It is not laziness. It is effort landing in the wrong place. I had assumed the problem was that I needed more words. The words were there. What I was not doing was using them anywhere uncomfortable. The inflection point was not a course and it was not a book. It was being asked to chair a call I had attended silently for two years. I was worse at it than I wanted to be, and the following month I was measurably better. One last thing, and it is the practical one. Keep a short record of what you handled, with dates on it. You forget very quickly what you could not do six months ago, and when somebody asks you for evidence, a feeling is not going to help you.

extra_audio.text: Rather than tell you it is going well, let me take stock of where this actually stands. In June I gave the read-out live and took eleven minutes of questions. Written work has not moved since March, and that is the plateau. So the second half consolidates, and I will set one demonstrable milestone for December.

reading.rtitle: Mid-Programme Development Note -- Commercial Directorate, Brazil
paras: This note takes stock at the midpoint of a plan agreed in January. It is written from observation rather than from self-report: three meetings were attended and the quarterly read-out of June was reviewed in full.

The trajectory on spoken performance is clear. In January the quarterly read-out was drafted by the regional team and delivered as written. In June it was delivered live, and eleven minutes of questions were taken without the meeting reverting to another language. What has changed is not the range of vocabulary, which was never the constraint. It is the structure: the signposting that used to be visibly chosen now appears to be second nature.

Written output is the plateau. The same regional directive has been drafted three times since March, and it is the third version that is circulated. Milan raised this in April; it was not raised by the director herself, and it should have been. That omission is recorded here because a midpoint review that lists only gains is of no use to anybody.

The recommendation for the second half is consolidation rather than expansion. One demonstrable milestone should be set for December, with the evidence defined in advance. On the evidence available, the spoken work would appear to hold under pressure and requires maintenance rather than attention; the writing is where the step change has to come from.
